recipes.name: Launch a new product or service
recipes.outcome: A tiered launch plan, positioning, launch assets and a day-by-day run sheet, ready to go live.
recipes.when_to_use: You have a new product, service or offer going live in the next two to eight weeks and want the positioning, launch assets and a day-by-day plan handled, so launch day is calm instead of chaotic.

inputs_from_owner.label: What you are launching, who it is for and the price
inputs_from_owner.example: A $49/month meal-prep subscription for busy parents in two postcodes

inputs_from_owner.label: Target go-live date and any fixed moments (event, season, trade show)
inputs_from_owner.example: Soft launch 3 March to existing customers, public launch 10 March

inputs_from_owner.label: What a successful launch looks like, in numbers
inputs_from_owner.example: 150 paid sign-ups in the first 30 days

inputs_from_owner.label: Channels you already have: email list, social accounts, store, sales team
inputs_from_owner.example: 4,200 email subscribers, 9k Instagram followers, no paid ads yet

inputs_from_owner.label: Launch budget and any spending limits
inputs_from_owner.example: $3,000 for ads and one photo shoot

inputs_from_owner.label: Beta results, early customer quotes or reviews we may use (with permission)
inputs_from_owner.example: 12 beta families, average rating 4.8/5, three quotes approved

composition.why: Samuel tiers the launch, sets the go/no-go gate and makes sure the market, the team and customers all understand the offer on day one.
Meera sharpens the positioning and messaging house first, so every asset repeats one promise instead of six.
Andre writes the launch page and announcement emails with the boldest claims the proof can carry.
Leilani turns the launch story into platform-native posts and short videos people actually stop for.
Anita counts back from launch day, owns the run sheet and says so plainly when something turns red.
Susan reviews the positioning, where a wrong promise costs most, and runs the pre-mortem so the launch has early warnings and a plan B.

plan_skeleton.title: Sharpen positioning and the messaging house
plan_skeleton.acceptance: All five positioning components are filled with evidence; the messaging house has one core promise, three pillars and at least two proof points per pillar; the reviewer's first line is APPROVED.
plan_skeleton.brief: Use the offer summary, early proof and what memory holds about existing customers. Name the alternative the buyer uses today, then build the messaging house that every later asset must quote.

plan_skeleton.title: Tier the launch and set numeric goals
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Launch tier (1-3) with rationale, numeric goals, channels per tier, owners and a go/no-go gate; the owner has confirmed the tier and the date.
plan_skeleton.brief: Match effort to stakes: a tier-1 launch uses every channel, a tier-3 launch gets an email and an update. Ask the owner to confirm tier and date before any asset is made.

plan_skeleton.title: Write the launch page and announcement emails
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Launch page copy and a three-email announcement sequence use messaging-house wording; every claim maps to a proof point; a LIFT review of the page leaves no high-severity issue open.
plan_skeleton.brief: One goal and one call to action per email (AIDA or PAS). On mobile, the first screen of the page must say what it is, who it is for and why now.

plan_skeleton.title: Make launch posts and short videos
plan_skeleton.acceptance: At least ten platform-native posts and two short-video scripts with storyboards cover the launch fortnight, each with alt text and a hook in the first two seconds; all are drafts awaiting owner approval.
plan_skeleton.brief: Pace posts to the run sheet: tease, reveal, proof, last call. Nothing is scheduled or published without the owner's approval.

plan_skeleton.title: Build the day-by-day run sheet
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Run sheet from T-14 to T+7 with an owner and time for every item, a pause or rollback step for each channel, and a go/no-go checklist the owner can tick.
plan_skeleton.brief: Include the dependencies (stock, pages live, payment tested, support briefed) and the moment each owner approval is needed.

plan_skeleton.title: Run the launch pre-mortem
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Top five failure modes ranked by likelihood and impact, each with an early-warning signal and a mitigation added to the run sheet with a named owner.
plan_skeleton.brief: Imagine it is T+7 and the launch flopped. Work back to causes, then make sure each one has a signal and a fix in the run sheet.

deliverables.name: Positioning canvas and messaging house
deliverables.description: The promise, pillars, proof and say-this-not-that list that every asset follows.

deliverables.name: Tiered launch plan
deliverables.description: Tier, numeric goals, channels, owners and the go/no-go gate.

deliverables.name: Launch page copy
deliverables.description: Page copy in page order, with the LIFT review notes.

deliverables.name: Announcement email sequence
deliverables.description: Three emails with subject-line and preheader variants, ready for owner approval.

deliverables.name: Launch fortnight posts
deliverables.description: Platform-native posts with visuals and alt text, as drafts.

deliverables.name: Day-by-day run sheet
deliverables.description: T-14 to T+7 with owners, times, approvals and rollback steps.

deliverables.name: Go/no-go record
deliverables.description: The owner's decision, the conditions attached and who confirmed each check.

meeting_moments.title: Launch kickoff: what are we really launching?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Samuel frames the goal and the tier options, Meera names the one-sentence promise she will test, Anita counts back from launch day, and Susan asks which day-7 number would make us pause.

meeting_moments.title: Does the promise survive a sceptic?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Susan plays a busy prospect who has never heard of you. Meera defends the positioning with customer evidence, and Andre tests whether it can be said in one line.

meeting_moments.title: Go / no-go
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: The top five risks and their fixes, the checklist status and a clear go, go-with-conditions or wait recommendation. You make the call; nothing goes live without it.

duration_estimate.note: Plus owner approvals; assets are ready at least a week before launch day.

lines: Tier 2 launch: goal 60 sign-ups in 14 days; go/no-go on Thursday at 4 pm.
Day -3: staff briefed and the FAQ live; Day 0 9:00: page live, email to 1,840 subscribers, first post.
Day 2: short video 2 of 4 and the first customer quote; Day 5: reminder email to non-openers only.
Owner decisions: launch price and the date; everything else has an owner and a time.

success_criteria: Every launch asset quotes the approved messaging house; no asset introduces a new promise.
The owner confirmed the launch tier, date and numeric goal before any asset was produced.
The run sheet has a named owner, a time and a rollback step for every channel from T-14 to T+7.
Each of the top five pre-mortem risks has an early-warning signal and an owner in the run sheet.
Nothing was published, scheduled or sent without a recorded owner approval.

variants_by_industry.changes: Adds release notes, a beta cohort and an in-product announcement, with tiers set by feature impact. Yara replaces Leilani so support macros and docs are ready on launch day.
Adds product pages, collection placement and a launch bundle. Chloe writes the listings and the run sheet includes stock and fulfilment checks.
For a new menu, venue or service: George costs the new items to the plate, and the run sheet covers a staff tasting, training and a soft-opening night.
For a course or cohort: Nicole designs the curriculum backwards from learner outcomes, and the launch sells a pilot cohort before the full programme.
For a new class, membership or studio: Javier sets intro offers that fill classes without cheapening membership, and the plan adds a founding-member week.
Launching a maintenance membership: the price book, the visit schedule, a presale to past customers and technician scripts.

recipes.name: Positioning & messaging sprint
recipes.outcome: Sharpened positioning, a messaging house and rewritten homepage copy the whole business can use.
recipes.when_to_use: Prospects keep asking what you actually do, you keep competing on price, or your homepage could belong to any competitor. Run it before a launch, a rebrand, a raise or a new sales push.

inputs_from_owner.label: Three to five of your best-fit customers and why they chose you
inputs_from_owner.example: Two dental groups and a physio chain that switched from spreadsheets

inputs_from_owner.label: What customers would do if you didn't exist (competitors, DIY, doing nothing)
inputs_from_owner.example: A big national agency, a freelancer, or the owner doing it at night

inputs_from_owner.label: Your current homepage
inputs_from_owner.example: https://example.com

inputs_from_owner.label: Reviews, call recordings, testimonials or survey answers we can read
inputs_from_owner.example: Google reviews plus six recorded sales calls in Zoom

inputs_from_owner.label: Words, claims or brand elements that must stay
inputs_from_owner.example: Keep the name and the 'no lock-in' promise

composition.why: Meera runs the positioning method end to end and owns the messaging house the whole business will speak from.
Claire mines reviews and calls for the exact words customers use, so the positioning is built from evidence, not the team's opinions.
Andre turns the messaging house into homepage copy that makes people stop, nod and click.
Amy reviews the homepage for hesitation points and designs the test that proves the new version works.
Liam shows where competitors already stand and challenges any claim they could also make, so the positioning is distinct instead of merely nice.

plan_skeleton.title: Mine reviews and calls for customer language
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A coded dataset of at least 30 reviews, calls or interviews with the exact phrases customers use for pains, alternatives and outcomes; themes counted by source; personal data redacted.
plan_skeleton.brief: Read the owner's reviews, testimonials and recordings first, then public reviews of the alternatives. Keep verbatim quotes; note who switched from what, and why.

plan_skeleton.title: Tear down the real alternatives
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A side-by-side matrix of three to five real alternatives, including DIY or doing nothing, with sourced and dated pricing, claims and review themes, and where each one honestly beats us.
plan_skeleton.brief: Screenshots and public pages only. The honest 'where they win' column is required.

plan_skeleton.title: Draft the positioning canvas
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Canvas with competitive alternatives, unique attributes, value, best-fit customers and market category, each backed by a quote or teardown fact; the best-fit customer excludes someone specific; the owner picks between at most two category framings.
plan_skeleton.brief: Follow the Obviously Awesome order: alternatives first, category last. Show the owner the two strongest category framings and what each implies.

plan_skeleton.title: Build the messaging house
plan_skeleton.acceptance: One core message, three pillars with at least two proof points each, audience variants for the top two segments and a say-this-not-that list of ten pairs; saved to memory for every coworker.
plan_skeleton.brief: Proof points must be things customers said or facts we can show. Save the house to memory so every coworker uses it by default.

plan_skeleton.title: Rewrite the homepage
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Homepage copy in page order (hero, proof, how it works, objections, call to action) using messaging-house wording; every claim traces to a proof point; the LIFT review shows no high-severity friction.
plan_skeleton.brief: Write the hero three ways and keep the one a stranger understands in five seconds. Answer the top two objections near the call to action.

plan_skeleton.title: Plan the homepage test
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A pre-registered test of the new hero against the old with primary metric, sample size and stop rule; if traffic is too low for an A/B test, it says so and uses a five-second or preference test instead.
plan_skeleton.brief: Check traffic first. Low-traffic sites get a qualitative test with five target customers rather than an underpowered A/B test.

deliverables.name: Customer evidence file
deliverables.description: Coded quotes by theme and source, with personal data removed.

deliverables.name: Alternatives matrix
deliverables.description: Offer, pricing, claims and review themes for each alternative, sourced and dated.

deliverables.name: Messaging house
deliverables.description: Core message, pillars, proof, audience variants and say-this-not-that list.

deliverables.name: Homepage copy
deliverables.description: Copy in page order with the LIFT notes.

meeting_moments.title: Why do your best customers choose you?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Meera and Claire interview you for twenty minutes about your best customers, the deals you lost and what you would never do. You can join live or let them work from your notes.

meeting_moments.title: Different, or just nice?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Liam reads each claim and asks whether a competitor could say it too. Claire answers with customer quotes, and Meera ends with the two category framings for you to choose between.

meeting_moments.title: Five-second test, read aloud
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Andre reads the new hero aloud, Amy says where a visitor would hesitate, and the team agrees the version to test.

duration_estimate.note: Faster if reviews and call recordings are available through connectors.

lines: Customers compare us with 'doing it themselves', not with the big agency.
What only we do: same-week installs with one named technician from quote to handover.
Best-fit customer: homeowners renovating one room who have been let down before.
Statement: For homeowners who can't face another no-show, we install in the week we promise, with one person you can call.

success_criteria: Every positioning component cites at least one customer quote or competitor fact.
The best-fit customer definition excludes someone specific; it is not 'everyone'.
The new homepage hero passes a five-second test by someone outside the team: they can say what it is and who it is for.
The messaging house is saved to memory so every coworker uses it by default.
The owner chose the market category framing, and the rejected option is recorded with the reason.

variants_by_industry.changes: Samuel joins to turn the positioning into a sales narrative and battlecards for the top two competitors.
Positioning usually means a narrower niche. Jack checks the niche against current client margins and utilisation, so the firm isn't positioned away from its best work.
Filip checks the words locals actually search for, and the homepage rewrite doubles as the Google Business Profile description.
Chloe carries the positioning into product titles and descriptions for the top sellers.

recipes.name: Brand refresh
recipes.outcome: A refreshed identity kit, voice guide and applied samples across web, social and print.
recipes.when_to_use: Your look feels dated or inconsistent, you've outgrown a DIY logo, or you're moving upmarket, and you want a refresh that keeps the recognition you've earned rather than a risky rebrand. If the name or the mark itself changes, use the full team so a trademark knockout search goes to your attorney.

inputs_from_owner.label: Current logo files, colours, fonts and photos
inputs_from_owner.example: Logo as PNG and AI, two brand colours, whatever fonts the website uses

inputs_from_owner.label: Who you want to appeal to now, compared with when the brand was made
inputs_from_owner.example: From students to young professionals who book corporate classes

inputs_from_owner.label: Elements customers recognise and you want to keep
inputs_from_owner.example: The orange and the fox in the logo

inputs_from_owner.label: Where the brand must work: storefront, van, packaging, website, social, uniforms
inputs_from_owner.example: Shopfront sign, website, Instagram, takeaway bags

inputs_from_owner.label: Brands you admire and brands you do not want to look like
inputs_from_owner.example: Admire: calm Scandinavian cafés. Avoid: fast-food red and yellow

composition.why: Nadia turns the refresh into one sharp idea and a brief every maker can execute, and runs critiques that make the work better.
Meera writes the voice guide and keeps the refresh tied to who the business is for now.
Jose evolves the logo, palette and type into a system that holds up from favicon to storefront.
Anna makes the print samples print right the first time, with correct bleed, colour and specs.
Camille reviews the identity for accessible contrast, type and documents (WCAG 2.2) and for inclusive imagery and language, so the refresh welcomes everyone it should.
Susan reviews the identity as the owner's oldest customer would, so the brave route still reads in two seconds and keeps the recognition you've earned.

plan_skeleton.title: Audit every live touchpoint
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Every live touchpoint (web, social, print, signage) is captured and scored against current rules; the equity to keep and the inconsistencies to fix are named with screenshots.
plan_skeleton.brief: Collect screenshots and photos of everything customers see. Separate what customers recognise (keep) from what is just inconsistent (fix).

plan_skeleton.title: Write the brief and moodboards
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A one-page brief (audience insight, single-minded proposition, mandatories, what must not change) and two or three moodboard directions; the owner picks one direction or a named hybrid.
plan_skeleton.brief: Each direction evolves the existing equity; none starts from zero. Show each direction applied to one real touchpoint.

plan_skeleton.title: Write the voice and style guide
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Three to five voice attributes with this-not-that pairs, tone by situation, a word list, mechanics and at least five before/after rewrites of the owner's real copy.
plan_skeleton.brief: Rewrite real copy the owner already uses (homepage hero, an email, a sign) to prove the guide works.

plan_skeleton.title: Design the refreshed identity kit
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Refined logo lock-ups (primary, stacked, icon) evolved from the current mark, a colour system where every text pairing passes WCAG 2.2 contrast (4.5:1 body, 3:1 large), an open-licence type pairing and usage rules; an old/new comparison shows recognition kept.
plan_skeleton.brief: Refine, don't replace: keep the recognisable elements from the audit. Test the icon at favicon size and the colours in greyscale.

plan_skeleton.title: Apply the kit to web and social
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Five reusable social templates and a website hero mock-up in the new system, sized to each platform's safe zones, with alt text and copy in the new voice.
plan_skeleton.brief: Templates must be editable by the owner. Use real copy in the new voice, not placeholder text.

plan_skeleton.title: Produce print-ready samples
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Print-ready samples (business card, one flyer or menu, one sign) at 300 dpi with bleed and CMYK specs; preflight passed; copy in the new voice.
plan_skeleton.brief: Choose samples from the owner's touchpoint list. Flag any finish that adds a print plate or cost.

deliverables.name: Touchpoint audit
deliverables.description: What to keep, what to fix, with screenshots.

deliverables.name: Brand guidelines and identity kit
deliverables.description: Logo lock-ups, colour system with contrast pairs, type, usage rules.

deliverables.name: Social templates and website hero mock-up

meeting_moments.title: What must never change?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Nadia walks you through what customers see today and asks what you love, what embarrasses you and what must never change. Join to steer, or listen while they work from your notes.

meeting_moments.title: Three directions, one choice
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Each direction applied to a real touchpoint, critiqued out loud. Susan asks which one your oldest customer would still recognise, and you choose.

meeting_moments.title: Does it still look like us?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: The old and new side by side. Sami reports the contrast results, Susan tests recognition, and Jose explains every change he kept or dropped.

duration_estimate.note: Includes two owner checkpoints; image generation makes this the costliest step.

lines: 23 live touchpoints reviewed: 4 logo versions, 6 greens and 3 typefaces in use.
Keep: the round mark and the deep green (customers recognise both in reviews).
Fix first: signage and van livery use an old logo; the web and print greens do not match.
Contrast: 5 of 12 colour pairs fail WCAG 2.2 AA for body text.

success_criteria: An old/new comparison shows the recognisable equity named in the audit was kept.
Every text and background colour pair in the palette passes WCAG 2.2 AA contrast (4.5:1 body, 3:1 large text).
The voice guide includes at least five before/after rewrites of the owner's real copy.
Applied samples exist for web, social and print, each built from the kit's templates.
The owner chose one creative direction before identity design began.

variants_by_industry.changes: Menus, signage and the storefront come first. George checks that the new menu layout still steers guests to the most profitable dishes.
Web and product matter more than print: Yuki carries the new identity into UI tokens and components, and Anna steps out.

Packaging and product photography lead. Jasmine sets the photo style so the store, the box and the ads look like one brand. Lucy checks any green or 'natural' claim on packaging and pages against evidence before it prints.
Channel art, thumbnails and a media kit replace print. Sasha keeps thumbnails recognisable at small sizes.

recipes.name: 90-day content engine
recipes.outcome: A content strategy, 90-day calendar and the first two weeks of produced, on-brand content.
recipes.when_to_use: You know you should publish regularly but it keeps slipping. You want a plan grounded in what customers actually ask, in your own voice, with the first two weeks already made so the habit starts now.

inputs_from_owner.label: Who you want to reach and what you want them to do next
inputs_from_owner.example: Owners of small building firms; book a site survey

inputs_from_owner.label: What content should do for the business (leads, search traffic, authority, retention)
inputs_from_owner.example: More enquiries from search within six months

inputs_from_owner.label: How much time you can give each week (interviews, reviews, filming)
inputs_from_owner.example: One 20-minute voice note a week and approvals on Fridays

inputs_from_owner.label: Where you publish today (blog, LinkedIn, newsletter, YouTube, Instagram)
inputs_from_owner.example: WordPress blog, LinkedIn, a quarterly newsletter

inputs_from_owner.label: Questions prospects and customers ask you most (or access to sales and support tools)
inputs_from_owner.example: How much does a loft conversion cost? Do I need planning permission?

composition.why: Adrian builds the strategy and calendar from real customer questions and writes the pillar pieces.
Filip maps the questions to keyword clusters and intent, so every piece has one job and no two compete.
Rahul interviews the owner and captures their voice, so the content sounds like the owner on their best day.
Leilani turns each pillar piece into platform-native posts and short videos.
Helen edits every piece to lead with the answer and hold to house style before anyone outside sees it.
Joyce is our sceptic on the scorecard: she insists on a baseline and a holdout, so we know which pieces bring customers rather than just traffic.

plan_skeleton.title: Map customer questions to keyword clusters
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Keyword clusters (pillar plus supporting) mapped to search intent and joined to real customer questions, with volume, difficulty and the page that should own each cluster; no two planned pieces target the same intent.
plan_skeleton.brief: Start from the questions sales and support hear (cost, problems, comparisons, reviews, best-of), then find the search demand behind them.

plan_skeleton.title: Interview the owner and capture their voice
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A 20-minute voice interview or set of voice notes transcribed, a voice fingerprint (phrases, rhythms, opinions), five story and opinion seeds with owner-approved facts, and two short posts in the owner's voice.
plan_skeleton.brief: Ask for stories, strong opinions and mistakes the owner has seen customers make. Nothing is attributed to the owner that they did not say or approve.

plan_skeleton.title: Build the strategy and 90-day calendar
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Three or four content pillars tied to the business goal, a 90-day calendar with owner, format, channel, target question or keyword and date for every item, a repurposing map and KPIs with a baseline; the owner approves a cadence they can sustain.
plan_skeleton.brief: Plan fewer, better pieces. Each long piece should feed at least five derivatives across channels.

plan_skeleton.title: Write the first two pillar pieces
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Two pillar articles written to intent, with first-hand experience from the owner interview, cited sources, internal links and meta title and description; the editor's first line is APPROVED.
plan_skeleton.brief: Answer the question in the first paragraph. Use the owner's stories as evidence of experience, never invented anecdotes.

plan_skeleton.title: Make two weeks of social derivatives
plan_skeleton.acceptance: At least eight platform-native posts and two short-video scripts derived from the pillar pieces, each with alt text; queued as drafts, nothing published without owner approval.
plan_skeleton.brief: Keep the owner's voice from the interview. Each post stands alone and links back to its pillar piece.

plan_skeleton.title: Set up the content scorecard
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A scorecard with organic sessions, assisted conversions and sign-ups per piece, UTM rules, a baseline and a 45-day checkpoint that states which result would change the plan.
plan_skeleton.brief: Measure assisted conversions, not just last click, and say plainly what content can and cannot be credited with.

deliverables.name: Content strategy
deliverables.description: Pillars, audience questions, channels, cadence and KPIs.

deliverables.name: 90-day content calendar
deliverables.description: Every item with owner, format, channel, keyword or question and date.

meeting_moments.title: Tell us what customers always ask
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Adrian and Rahul interview you about the questions you answer every week and the opinions you'd defend in public. Filip notes which ones people are already searching for.

meeting_moments.title: Editorial crit
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Helen edits the pillar pieces aloud, Filip checks they match what people search, and Elif asks how you will know they worked.

meeting_moments.title: Your 90-day plan in five minutes
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: A short voiced briefing: the pillars, what ships each week, what you need to give, and the day-45 checkpoint where the plan changes if the numbers say so.

duration_estimate.note: Needs one 20-minute owner interview; the calendar then runs on weekly approvals.

lines: Pillar 1: How much does a kitchen refit really cost? (840 searches a month, asked in 1 in 5 sales calls).
Week 1: the pillar article, 3 short videos cut from the owner interview, 4 posts and 1 newsletter.
Every piece answers a real customer question in the owner's own words; the source call is noted.
Scorecard: enquiries per piece against a holdout of untouched pages, not just views.

success_criteria: Every calendar item has an owner, format, channel, date and a target question or keyword.
Each pillar piece includes first-hand experience from the owner interview and cites its sources.
No two planned pieces target the same search intent.
Two weeks of content exist as approval-ready drafts, not ideas.
A day-45 checkpoint with the result that would change the plan is on the calendar.

variants_by_industry.changes: Cost, problem and comparison articles work especially well here. Sandra supplies honest price ranges from real jobs so the cost article is credible.
Expertise-led: more bylined thought leadership and anonymised case studies, fewer trend posts. Jack turns client questions into articles and checks nothing breaches client confidentiality.
Adds how-to, comparison and template content. Charlie writes the tutorials so marketing and documentation share one source, and Leilani steps out.
Video-first: the pillar piece is a video or episode and articles are derivatives. Sasha packages titles and thumbnails before production.
Lessons double as lead magnets: Nicole shapes pillar pieces into mini-lessons that lead to the paid programme.

recipes.name: SEO growth sprint
recipes.outcome: An SEO audit, keyword clusters, a fix list and four optimized pages.
recipes.when_to_use: Organic traffic has stalled or never started, you're invisible for searches your customers make, or a site change hurt your rankings.

inputs_from_owner.label: Your website address
inputs_from_owner.example: https://example.com

inputs_from_owner.label: Products, services or locations that matter most
inputs_from_owner.example: Emergency plumbing, boiler installs, three towns

inputs_from_owner.label: Which CMS you use and who can make changes
inputs_from_owner.example: WordPress; our web person can edit templates

inputs_from_owner.label: Access to Google Search Console and analytics (connector)
inputs_from_owner.example: Search Console and GA4 connected

inputs_from_owner.label: Competitors who rank where you want to
inputs_from_owner.example: Two regional firms and a national directory

composition.why: Filip finds why search engines can't see you and builds the keyword clusters and fix list.
Adrian rewrites the four target pages to answer the searcher's real question better than anyone ranking now.
Pim measures Core Web Vitals and turns the technical fixes into changes your site can actually ship.
Khalid sets the baseline and checks that the tracking fires, so in 90 days we can see whether the sprint moved enquiries, not just rankings.
Amy reviews the rewritten pages so ranking gains don't cost conversions; she holds the line where SEO depth and a clear call to action collide.

plan_skeleton.title: Run the SEO audit and build keyword clusters
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Indexability, on-page and cannibalisation issues listed with URL-level evidence joined to Search Console data; keyword clusters mapped to intent and to one target URL each; fix list ranked by impact and effort.
plan_skeleton.brief: Crawl the site, join Search Console queries to pages, and propose the four pages with the best upside for the owner's priority offers.

plan_skeleton.title: Measure Core Web Vitals on key templates
plan_skeleton.acceptance: LCP, INP and CLS measured on the top templates for mobile and desktop, with the three fixes most likely to move each metric and the effort for each.
plan_skeleton.brief: Measure real templates (home, service or category, article). No redesigns; name the smallest changes with the biggest effect.

plan_skeleton.title: Record the baseline and checkpoints
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Baseline clicks, impressions, average position and conversions for each target cluster, with 30/60/90-day checkpoints and the result that counts as success.
plan_skeleton.brief: Conversions and enquiries matter more than rankings. Note seasonality so the 90-day read is fair.

plan_skeleton.title: Rewrite the four target pages
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Four pages rewritten or created to match their cluster's intent: title, H1, meta description, structured headings, internal links, FAQ and schema suggestions and first-hand proof; each keeps or improves its conversion path.
plan_skeleton.brief: Confirm the four pages with the owner before writing. Keep the call to action visible; depth goes below it.

plan_skeleton.title: Prepare the technical fix pack
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Top technical fixes delivered as a reviewed diff with tests where the site is in a repository, or as step-by-step CMS instructions otherwise; nothing is deployed without owner approval.
plan_skeleton.brief: Redirects, canonicals, image sizes and render-blocking scripts first. Each fix lists how to roll it back.

deliverables.name: SEO audit
deliverables.description: Issues with URL-level evidence and the ranked fix list.

plan_skeleton.acceptance: Letters by segment that lead with value, state the new price and date plainly, explain the options and give a contact; a staff FAQ for pushback; no fake urgency.

plan_skeleton.title: Build the three-statement model
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Linked P&L, balance sheet and cash flow (monthly for 24 months, then annual to year 5) driven by labelled assumptions; the balance sheet balances every period; base and downside cases; use of funds tied to milestones.
plan_skeleton.brief: Model the owner's own plan. Every assumption is visible and changeable; no hidden plugs.

plan_skeleton.title: Size the market
plan_skeleton.acceptance: TAM, SAM and SOM bottom-up and top-down, triangulated, with every assumption sourced in a labelled cell; the SOM is reachable with the plan's own sales capacity.
plan_skeleton.brief: Defensible beats big. Show ranges, not false precision.

plan_skeleton.title: Model ownership scenarios
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Pre- and post-money ownership for the owner's own scenarios (SAFE conversion, priced round, option pool top-up), reconciled to the cap table to the share and labelled as mechanics, not advice.
plan_skeleton.brief: Explain how each instrument converts. Never recommend a valuation, instrument or term.

plan_skeleton.title: Write the investment narrative
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A one-page narrative (why now, why us, traction, the ask and use of funds) with the weaknesses stated plainly, and a slide-by-slide storyline the deck will follow.
plan_skeleton.brief: Every claim must be backed by the model or a source. Name the risks before an investor does.

plan_skeleton.title: Build the pitch deck
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A 12-to-15-slide deck (problem, solution, why now, market, traction, business model, go-to-market, competition, team, financials, the ask) with action titles, sourced charts and speaker notes; every number matches the model.
plan_skeleton.brief: One idea per slide. Charts come from the model, not retyped.

plan_skeleton.title: Assemble the data-room index
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A data-room index by category (corporate, cap table, financials, customers, IP, team, legal) with document status, owner and the gaps to fix before anyone asks.
plan_skeleton.brief: Index and status only; documents stay where the owner keeps them until the owner decides to share.

plan_skeleton.title: Run the diligence drill
plan_skeleton.acceptance: The 20 hardest diligence questions, each with the owner's evidence-backed answer or a named gap, and every deck claim marked supported, weak or unsupported.
plan_skeleton.brief: Steelman the sceptical investor. Weak claims get fixed or cut, not spun.

plan_skeleton.title: Licensed review before any investor sees it
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Deck, model, ownership scenarios and data-room index packaged for the owner's attorney and a licensed financial adviser with the questions to ask; nothing is sent to an investor until the owner records the outcome.
plan_skeleton.brief: Jane packages the deck, narrative and data-room index for a securities attorney, with Diana's model assumptions for a licensed financial adviser; nothing reaches an investor before both reviews are recorded.

recipes.name: Fundraising or grant campaign
recipes.outcome: A funder-matched grant proposal or donor campaign with stewardship plan and impact story.
recipes.when_to_use: Your nonprofit or social enterprise needs a grant application or a donor appeal done well: the right funders, a proposal that scores, an honest impact story and a plan that keeps donors giving.

inputs_from_owner.label: Your mission and the programme that needs funding
inputs_from_owner.example: After-school literacy programme for 120 children in two neighbourhoods

inputs_from_owner.label: How much you need, what it pays for and by when
inputs_from_owner.example: $85,000 for one year of staff and books, applications due 15 May

inputs_from_owner.label: Outcomes, numbers and stories you have (with permission to share)
inputs_from_owner.example: Reading levels up 1.4 grades on average; two families agreed to share their story

inputs_from_owner.label: Programme budget or last year's accounts
inputs_from_owner.example: Budget spreadsheet and last audited accounts

inputs_from_owner.label: A specific funder, call for proposals or donor list, if you have one

composition.why: Maria matches funders to your mission and builds donor relationships that outlast any single campaign.
Kate writes the proposal to score: every requirement mapped, the logic model clear, and 'why you' on page one.
Rahul writes the impact story and appeal letter in your leader's voice, with dignity for the people in the story.
Stefan builds the programme budget with restricted and unrestricted funds kept apart, so every line ties to an activity a funder can see.
Ibrahim grades every outcome claim against your own data and reviews the proposal and story, because an overstated claim can cost you the funder's trust for years.
Bruno keeps donor data to what stewardship needs, with consent for every contact and nothing compiled beyond it.

plan_skeleton.title: Match funders or donor segments
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Five to ten funders with mission fit, typical grant size, deadlines and eligibility, each sourced, with a go/no-go per funder; or, for a donor campaign, donor segments and ask amounts drawn from giving history.
plan_skeleton.brief: Fit beats volume. For donor campaigns, use aggregate giving data; keep personal details inside the owner's systems.

plan_skeleton.title: Grade the impact evidence
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Need-statement data with citations, and every outcome claim graded strong, moderate or weak against the organisation's own data; unsupported claims rewritten or cut.
plan_skeleton.brief: Say exactly what the data shows and how sure we can be. Honest claims are more persuasive to experienced funders.

plan_skeleton.title: Build the programme budget
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A programme budget with direct and indirect costs, match or in-kind lines, restricted and unrestricted funds marked, and a budget narrative that ties every line to an activity in the logic model.
plan_skeleton.brief: Ask honestly for the true cost, including overheads. Every figure must reconcile to the organisation's accounts.

plan_skeleton.title: Write the funder-matched proposal
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Proposal with a compliance matrix against the call, need statement, logic model (inputs to outcomes), evaluation plan, sustainability section and budget narrative; every requirement mapped to a page.
plan_skeleton.brief: Mirror the funder's language and scoring criteria. Use only graded claims.

plan_skeleton.title: Write the impact story and appeal
plan_skeleton.acceptance: One impact story told with the participant's recorded permission and dignity, an appeal letter in the leader's voice and a three-email donor sequence; every number matches the evidence file.
plan_skeleton.brief: People are protagonists, not props. Change identifying details unless the person agreed to be named.

plan_skeleton.title: Plan donor and funder stewardship
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A moves-management plan by segment (identify, qualify, cultivate, solicit, steward) with thank-yous within 48 hours, impact reports and a 12-month calendar of touches.
plan_skeleton.brief: Stewardship is where next year's gift is won. Keep it realistic for the team's time.

plan_skeleton.title: Licensed review of gift language and donor data
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Gift-acknowledgement and restricted-fund wording go to the organisation's accountant and donor-data handling to its privacy adviser, with the questions to answer; nothing is submitted or sent until the owner records the outcome.
plan_skeleton.brief: Coworkers organise and draft; tax treatment of gifts and data-protection questions are for qualified professionals.

meeting_moments.title: Tell us the story only you can tell
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Maria and Rahul interview you about the programme, the people it serves and the moment you knew it worked; Ibrahim asks what data backs it up.

meeting_moments.title: Score it like a funder

meeting_moments.title: Your campaign in five minutes
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: A short voiced briefing: which funders, what we're asking for, the story we're telling, the stewardship calendar and what's waiting on your accountant's review.

duration_estimate.note: Grant deadlines set the pace; allow time for the licensed review.

recipes.name: PR push
recipes.outcome: Story angles, a press kit, a targeted media list and tailored pitches ready to send on approval.
recipes.when_to_use: You have real news (a launch, a milestone, research, a community story) or want to be known as the expert in your field, and you want coverage from the right five journalists rather than a blast to five hundred.

inputs_from_owner.label: What happened, or what you can say that is new
inputs_from_owner.example: We opened our second site and hired 14 local people

inputs_from_owner.label: Numbers, customers or data that back it up
inputs_from_owner.example: 1,000 customers in year one; two customers happy to be quoted

inputs_from_owner.example: The founder, mornings next week

inputs_from_owner.label: Outlets or journalists you'd love to be in
inputs_from_owner.example: The city paper and two trade magazines

inputs_from_owner.label: Any embargo date or event to tie in

composition.why: Karen shapes one clear story, the key messages and who hears it first, so staff and customers aren't surprised by the press.
Lukas finds the real news, writes the press kit and pitches the right five journalists, not five hundred.
Rahul writes a bylined article in the spokesperson's own voice, with a point of view rather than an advert.
Laura checks every claim, number and quote against primary sources before anything reaches a journalist.
Aman is our sceptic on the key messages: he asks who could be hurt or misled by each claim before a reporter does.

plan_skeleton.title: Test the news and find the angle
plan_skeleton.acceptance: The news test is passed (new, relevant, timely, human, surprising) or the team says honestly it isn't news yet and what would make it news; three angles ranked by fit for target beats; the owner picks one.
plan_skeleton.brief: Think like an editor: why would their readers care this week?

plan_skeleton.title: Set key messages and who hears first
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Three key messages with proof, a one-line 'what this means for readers', and a sequence so staff and key customers hear before the press.
plan_skeleton.brief: Nobody important should learn this news second-hand.

plan_skeleton.title: Write the press kit
plan_skeleton.acceptance: An AP-style release with an active headline and 5Ws lede, quotes approved by the people quoted, a fact sheet, boilerplate, bios and an image list with credits; every fact verified.
plan_skeleton.brief: Quotes must add meaning, not adjectives. Every quote is approved by the person quoted.

plan_skeleton.title: Write a bylined article
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A 700-to-900-word op-ed or bylined article in the spokesperson's voice that adds a point of view, with every claim sourced and the spokesperson's approval recorded.
plan_skeleton.brief: Interview the spokesperson briefly by voice. It must read as their opinion, not a press release.

plan_skeleton.title: Build the media list and tailored pitches
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A tiered list of 10 to 25 journalists, each with the recent article that proves they cover the beat, and a short personalised pitch for each tier-one contact; nothing is sent until the owner approves each pitch.
plan_skeleton.brief: Journalists' public professional details only. Tailor each pitch to what that journalist actually writes.

plan_skeleton.title: Prepare the spokesperson
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Key messages, bridging lines and a 15-question hostile drill, run as a voiced mock interview with the spokesperson and debriefed with three improvements.
plan_skeleton.brief: Rehearse the question they least want to be asked until the answer is calm and true.

deliverables.name: Media list
deliverables.description: Journalists with the recent article that proves the fit.

meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Eva plays a tough journalist. Join as the spokesperson to practise, or listen as Lukas and Karen coach the answers between rounds.

The spokesperson has rehearsed the hostile questions in a voiced mock interview.
No pitch is sent without the owner's approval.

plan_skeleton.title: Design the event concept and agenda

plan_skeleton.title: Write invites, reminders and follow-up

recipes.name: New market entry study
recipes.outcome: Market sizing, a competitor map, go-to-market options and a go/no-go recommendation.
recipes.when_to_use: You're weighing a new city, country, customer segment or channel and want evidence before you commit money, sign a lease or hire.

inputs_from_owner.label: The market you're considering and why now
inputs_from_owner.example: Opening in Manchester; two customers there asked us to

inputs_from_owner.label: What you sell today and your current numbers
inputs_from_owner.example: Two studios in Leeds, 600 members, 22% margin

inputs_from_owner.label: How much you could invest and how long you could wait for payback
inputs_from_owner.example: Up to £150k, payback within two years

inputs_from_owner.label: Hard constraints (timing, licences, people who must be involved)
inputs_from_owner.example: Must open before January; head coach relocates

inputs_from_owner.label: Anything you already know about the market
inputs_from_owner.example: Three competitors near the station; rents rising

composition.why: Stella frames the entry as a few hard choices, including where not to play, and writes the go/no-go recommendation.
Mateo sizes the market bottom-up with every assumption in a cell you can change.
Liam maps the local competitors and substitutes, with sourced pricing and what their customers complain about.
Sophie finds the licences, permits and rules that apply, from primary sources, with lead times.
Diana models the entry economics: capital needed, break-even month, payback and the downside case.
Kenji tests the recommendation against four plausible futures, so the go decision survives whichever one arrives.

plan_skeleton.title: Size the market and segments
plan_skeleton.acceptance: TAM, SAM and SOM bottom-up and top-down for the target market with every assumption in a labelled, sourced cell, ranges rather than points, and segments ranked by size and reachability.
plan_skeleton.brief: Start from reachable customers and realistic adoption, then check against top-down sources.

plan_skeleton.title: Map competitors and substitutes
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Three to six local competitors and substitutes in a matrix (offer, normalised pricing, positioning, channels, review themes), sourced and dated, with the white space stated in one sentence.
plan_skeleton.brief: Include doing nothing and DIY. Public sources only.

plan_skeleton.title: Rate the industry forces
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Five forces rated for the bounded target market with cited evidence and the two or three implications for how to enter.
plan_skeleton.brief: Bound the industry tightly (this market, this offer) or the analysis says nothing.

plan_skeleton.title: Find the rules, licences and barriers
plan_skeleton.acceptance: The licences, permits, registrations and sector rules that apply, from primary sources with dates, lead times and costs; unknowns flagged as questions for local counsel.
plan_skeleton.brief: Never state a legal conclusion as certain; flag jurisdiction assumptions.

plan_skeleton.title: Model the entry economics
plan_skeleton.acceptance: For each entry option: capital needed, monthly P&L and cash to break-even, payback and a downside case, tied to the sizing assumptions and licence costs.
plan_skeleton.brief: Model the owner's own options. Show which assumption the answer is most sensitive to.

plan_skeleton.title: Compare entry options and recommend
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Two or three entry options (for example partner-led, pop-up test, full launch) scored on agreed criteria; a go, no-go or test-first recommendation with the conditions that would reverse it; stage gates with kill criteria.
plan_skeleton.brief: Name what the owner gives up with each option. The owner makes the call.

plan_skeleton.title: Licensed review of legal and licensing findings
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Regulatory findings and open questions packaged for local counsel in the target market; the owner records the outcome before any lease, registration, hire or public announcement.
plan_skeleton.brief: Prepare the questions; counsel decides. The study itself commits the owner to nothing.

meeting_moments.title: What would make this a yes?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Stella sets the decision and the criteria, Mateo explains how we'll size the market, Diana asks about your money and patience, and Kenji names the futures we'll test against.

meeting_moments.title: Go, no-go or test first?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Stella argues for her recommendation; Kenji runs it through four futures and Diana through the downside case. You hear where they still disagree.

meeting_moments.title: Your call
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: The recommendation, the stage gates and the questions waiting on local counsel. You decide; the decision and its reversal conditions are recorded.

duration_estimate.note: Plus local counsel's review before any commitment.

recipes.name: Video or podcast series pilot

inputs_from_owner.example: Help first-time landlords trust us before they need a letting agent

inputs_from_owner.label: Who it's for
inputs_from_owner.example: People who just bought their first rental flat

inputs_from_owner.example: Me plus a coworker co-host

plan_skeleton.title: Write the series bible
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A series bible with the promise, audience, format (length, segments, cadence), host roles, recurring segments, ten episode ideas ranked and success metrics per platform; the owner picks the format and pilot topic.
plan_skeleton.brief: One sentence should explain why someone would subscribe. Design for the audience's real listening moments.

plan_skeleton.title: Package the pilot before scripting
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Ten title options and three thumbnail concepts for the pilot (one focal subject, at most four words, high contrast), written before the script; two are carried forward.
plan_skeleton.brief: If we can't package it, we shouldn't make it. The script must pay off the chosen title.

plan_skeleton.title: Script the pilot
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A pilot script that pays off the title in the first 30 seconds, written for the ear, with segment timings, host lines in each host's voice and a source for every factual claim.
plan_skeleton.brief: Interview the owner briefly by voice for stories and opinions; nothing is put in the owner's mouth that they haven't approved.

plan_skeleton.title: Produce the voiced pilot
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A mixed pilot episode with each speaker in a distinct voice, loudness-normalised, with transcript and chapters; hosts are the owner's own recording or coworker voices, never a cloned voice.
plan_skeleton.brief: Coworker voices are clearly AI voices. The owner's voice is used only from their own recording.

plan_skeleton.title: Test the pilot with five listeners
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Five people from the target audience, invited by the owner with consent recorded, listen or watch; drop-off and attention moments logged with the top three fixes. If recruiting isn't possible, a walkthrough clearly labelled as not a user test.
plan_skeleton.brief: Ask where they would have skipped, and what they would tell a friend the show is about.

plan_skeleton.title: Cut the video version and clips
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A video version or audiogram of the revised pilot plus three vertical clips with a hook in the first two seconds and burned-in captions; final thumbnails from the chosen concepts; rights logged. The video version shows the speaking coworkers as lip-synced avatars with a burned-in 'AI coworker' label.
plan_skeleton.brief: Apply the listener-test fixes first. Clips must stand alone.

plan_skeleton.title: Plan the release
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A publishing checklist per platform (titles, descriptions, chapters, show notes), a four-week release calendar and the day-7 and day-30 numbers that decide whether to make a season; nothing is published without owner approval.
plan_skeleton.brief: Decide now what success looks like, so the season decision is easy.

deliverables.name: Voiced pilot episode
deliverables.description: With transcript and chapters.

meeting_moments.title: Make a season?
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: What the listener test showed, the revised pilot, the release plan and the numbers that decide a season. You decide whether and when to publish.

Nothing is published without the owner's approval.

plan_skeleton.title: Build the margin-safe promo calendar
plan_skeleton.acceptance: A six-month calendar tied to demand moments with maximum discount depth, a margin floor per promotion, code-leakage controls and the stock needed; past promotions' incremental lift and pull-forward shown.

inputs_from_owner.label: The result you want this quarter

inputs_from_owner.label: Current backlog or feature requests

plan_skeleton.title: Opportunity-solution tree

plan_skeleton.title: RICE-scored backlog

plan_skeleton.title: Now/next/later roadmap
plan_skeleton.acceptance: Now, next and later columns tied to outcomes, with what was deliberately stopped and the evidence that would move each parked item.

plan_skeleton.title: Measurement plan

meeting_moments.title: What should change for customers?

meeting_moments.title: Is the order right?

meeting_moments.title: Your roadmap
meeting_moments.what_owner_hears: Now, next and later on one page, what you're deliberately not doing, and how you'll know it worked.

Activation is measured from events verified to fire.

The owner can see what was deliberately stopped.
